programs.name: OPPD Business Rebate Program (HVAC Equipment Rebates, ARC, BMS, Retro-Commissioning, Custom Project Rebates)
programs.how: Online application software/portal; installation and submission through OPPD's approved Trade Ally network; custom projects start with a Custom Project Notification Form emailed to BusinessRebates@oppd.com
programs.mv: Custom projects: IPMVP Option A/B/C. Option A/B short-term sub-metering must include a minimum of 3 weeks of hot weather (pre/post kW trending); Option C uses OPPD bill comparison of June-September billing months post-completion vs baseline (no weather normalization for kW). Energy Study required for all custom projects; PE required for most optimization projects; project must show verified sustainable energy savings of at least 5% and 5-year persistence; OPPD reserves right to install metering on any rebated equipment.
programs.custom: $500 per actual kW of peak demand reduction, capped at 50% of total project cost, not to exceed $100,000 per project; 30% of expected kW rebate can be advanced at preapproval; Energy Study rebate up to 50% of study cost (max $10,000) (Business Rebate T&C, Jan 2026)
programs.presc: RTUs $100-$200/ton (EER-based); heat pumps $100-$200/ton plus $50/ton conversion adder; chillers $50-$300/ton; Advanced Rooftop Unit Controllers (ARC) $135-$207/ton from approved vendor list (existing buildings only, one-to-one with RTU, requires 3-year RTU service agreement per ASHRAE/ACCA 180-2018); BMS 20-30% of cost or $0.40-$0.60/sq ft (max $100k); Small Business BMS 40% or $0.75/sq ft (max $15k); retro-commissioning $0.10-$0.20/sq ft. Equipment rebates may be limited to 50% of material/equipment cost; $100,000 max per facility per calendar year.
programs.pay: Prescriptive: not stated for business (residential checks arrive in ~6 weeks; flag). Custom: slow by design - final payment is made only after the June-September OPPD billing months post project completion and case-study approval, so custom checks can lag completion by many months.
programs.budget: Calendar-year budget, first-come first-served; if exhausted the program goes 'SOLD OUT' and no applications or preapprovals are accepted until the software resets January 1-10 of the following year. Preapproved prescriptive funds reserved 120 days; preapproved projects >=$5,000 must complete within 3 months (BMS/RCx 12 months, custom up to 24 months).

programs.u: Nebraska Public Power District (NPPD) / EnergyWise Nebraska (with participating munis, PPDs and co-ops)
programs.name: EnergyWise Business Incentives (Commercial HVAC, Prescriptive & Custom Lighting, VFDs, Industrial Process, HVAC System Optimization)
programs.how: PDF application forms submitted to the customer's local retail electric utility after installation (with itemized invoices); incentive paid by local utility as check or bill credit at its discretion
programs.mv: Prescriptive measures: none beyond invoices/spec sheets. Custom (e.g., custom lighting, industrial process, HVAC System Optimization): pre-approval by an EnergyWise Energy Efficiency Consultant with an evaluation/energy-savings estimate; no published metering-duration requirement found (flag). Industrial process incentives based on documented annual energy savings.
programs.custom: Custom lighting: lesser of annual kWh savings x $0.07 or 50% of installation cost; industrial process: savings-based, capped at 50% of project costs. No published $/kWh rate for custom HVAC optimization (utility quotes incentive after evaluation).
programs.presc: Commercial HVAC $30-$330/ton (AC $30/ton; standard heat pumps $60-$120/ton; geothermal $330/ton); heat pump water heaters $400-$650; VFDs (1-200 hp, 2,000+ run-hours); smart thermostats. Residential-side cooling tune-up $30 exists but no published commercial RTU-controls or tune-up deemed measure.
programs.pay: Paid by local utility after installation, operational verification and completed application; no stated number of days (flag). Incentives >$5,000 must be pre-approved to guarantee funds; changes must be implemented and submitted for payment within one year of preapproval.
programs.budget: Annual EnergyWise program funded by NPPD wholesale participation; incentives >$5,000 need preapproval to guarantee fund availability; no facility may exceed $100,000/year in EnergyWise incentives without preapproval.

programs.name: LES Sustainable Energy Program (SEP)
programs.how: Participating contractor submits the project to LES on the customer's behalf after a signed quote; incentive delivered as an LES credit on the contractor's invoice; commercial customers directed to email SEP@les.com for application instructions
programs.presc: Commercial high-efficiency heat pumps and air conditioners are listed SEP measures (2025/2026 program documents exist) but per-ton amounts could not be verified - les.com blocks automated retrieval (403). Residential side: $1,000-ish LES heat pump incentives ($800 combinable with City of Lincoln incentives up to $3,800; heat pumps must be inverter-driven or >=15.2 SEER2 and >=12 EER2, AHRI rated); $500 heat pump water heater incentive for residential and commercial.
programs.pay: Effectively instant for the customer - incentive is applied as a credit on the participating contractor's invoice
programs.budget: 2026 funds available January 1 - December 31, 2026, first-come first-served, or until funds are expended, whichever comes first

states.apply_c: Essentially all commercial rebate activity in Delaware runs through one door: the DNREC EEIF online application portal (implemented by NV5), where the contractor can apply on the customer's behalf; the payee must also register in the State of Delaware eSupplier portal to get paid. Delmarva Power has no commercial prescriptive/custom rebate program of its own in Delaware today.
states.apply_r: Dominant design is Energize Delaware Home Performance with ENERGY STAR: an audit ($50/$25 customer cost) by a program-approved contractor is the gateway, then the contractor recommends and submits measure rebates; not an instant/midstream design. Delaware Electric Cooperative uses mail-in PDF applications; Delmarva's Delaware residential portfolio is mostly behavioral (home energy reports, check-ups).
states.trm: Delaware Technical Reference Manual (DNREC EEAC), Version 4.0 October 2024 (Version 5.0 draft July 2025); built on the Mid-Atlantic TRM v9 (NEEP)
states.rebate_c: Prescriptive HVAC $250-$1,500/ton depending on technology; custom $0.20-$0.30 per first-year kWh, both capped at 60% of efficiency-related project cost and $250,000 per address per year
states.rebate_r: HPwES (eff. 11/1/2024): central AC $650-$1,750; ducted heat pumps $800-$2,200; mini-splits $550-$1,700; smart thermostat $150-$200; capped at 50% of installed cost (75% for income-qualified Assisted track). DEC: $300 heat pump water heater.
states.ira: NOT launched as of mid-2026. DNREC's Home Energy Rebates page says both HER/HOMES ($2,000-$8,000 per home, savings-modeled) and HEAR ($500-$8,000, low-income electrification) are 'expected to launch once funding is received later this year,' still pending U.S. DOE funding/approval; up to $66M total for Delaware. Application was submitted August 2024 with launch originally expected Q2 2025 - roughly a year behind schedule.
flags: EEIF payment timeline (application-to-check) is not documented anywhere fetched; payment goes through the State of Delaware eSupplier system, which may add processing time - verify with NV5/DNREC (DCCE.EnergyRebates@NV5.com).
A third-party source stated EEIF is 'funded through June 30, 2026' (state fiscal year); the Feb 2026 guidelines are current, but confirm FY2027 funding continuation before building pipeline.

CRYOGENX4: the AC tune-up custom-pathway language covers charge adjustment/coil cleaning, not additives; guidelines also exclude 'routine maintenance procedures' and 'industrial technologies not approved by nationally recognized laboratories' - a DNREC eligibility ruling is needed before counting on this path.

HVAC OPTIMIZER controls-only projects are single-tier custom ($0.20/kWh); confirm whether a compressor-cycling controller counts as an EMS (which would unlock multi-tier $0.25/kWh) - guidelines say a device that only sets space/setback temperature is NOT an EMS.
TRM scan was of DE TRM v4.0 (Oct 2024); a v5.0 draft (July 2025) exists and was not fully scanned - small chance an ARC/RTU-controls measure was added.
Delaware Electric Cooperative commercial rebate offerings could not be confirmed (site returned 403); treated as residential-only pending direct contact.

Delmarva DE customers ARE eligible for EEIF (it is statewide, PUT-funded), so Delmarva's lack of its own commercial program does not block projects in its territory; municipal utility customers may see PUT coded as 'Commercial Tax'/'Utility Tax' - confirm PUT payment for muni-served leads before applying.
IRA HER/HEAR launch date is still unconfirmed ('later this year' per DNREC as fetched in July 2026); residential IRA revenue should not be assumed for 2026.
Delmarva 2027-2029 EE plan is pending PSC approval; even if approved it adds no commercial prescriptive/custom rebates - EEIF remains the only commercial rebate channel.
Instant/midstream residential rebates: no evidence found, scored as 'no', but Delmarva's online marketplace (secure.delmarva.com) may offer point-of-sale thermostat discounts - not verified.
states.notes_c: EEIF is unusually favorable: custom pre-approval is required but M&V is calculation-based (DNREC calculators, spec sheets, or P.E. stamp) with no stated pre/post metering requirement for non-CHP measures - a genuine opening for HVAC OPTIMIZER (single-tier $0.20/kWh; pairs with EMS/multiple end uses to reach $0.25-$0.30/kWh). CRYOGENX4 has a rare explicit hook: the guidelines state 'AC Tune-Up measures (e.g. refrigerant charge adjustment, coil cleaning, airflow adjustment)' on units >65 kBtu/h may be eligible for the custom pathway, itemized by activity; whether a refrigerant additive qualifies needs a DNREC ruling. Small-unit AC tune-ups (<65 kBtu/h) are prescriptive at $50/unit. Very-high-efficiency RTU replacement is classic deemed ($250/ton AC, $500-$1,000/ton HP, tiered IEER thresholds). No trade-ally network - contractor just needs a Delaware business license, trade license, and $1M CGL insurance. 3-year full warranty required on all granted equipment. Prescriptive pre-approval optional (can apply within 30 days after final invoice), custom pre-approval mandatory before any installation.
states.notes_r: HPwES requires the program-approved contractor network and an assessment before measure rebates; weatherization measures capped at 75% of cost. No evidence of a midstream/instant HVAC rebate channel in Delaware.

d.notes: Delaware's DESEU structure (non-utility statewide administrator under a public-purpose contract) is the same family as DCSEU and Hawaii Energy, but unlike DC's P4P program, no measured/NMEC-basis commercial track was found for Delaware.

programs.name: Energy Efficiency Investment Fund (EEIF) for Business - Prescriptive, Custom, Energy Assessment, and CHP pathways (implementer: NV5)
programs.how: Online EEIF Application Portal; contractor may submit on behalf of applicant; payee must also register in the State of Delaware eSupplier Portal before payment
programs.mv: Custom projects: documented savings via energy modeling, nameplate/spec data, DNREC-approved calculators, and/or P.E. signature; 12 consecutive months of utility bills at pre-approval; no pre/post metering duration specified for custom measures. Formal M&V plan required only for CHP systems >=800 kW. Applicant must allow evaluator access to facility energy-use data for 2 years post-install; pre/post inspections at DNREC discretion.
programs.custom: $0.20/kWh (single end-use), $0.25/kWh (multi-tier: 2 end uses or EMS), $0.30/kWh (comprehensive: 3+ end uses), plus $10-$27/MMBtu gas; capped at 60% of energy-efficiency-related cost and $250,000 per address per calendar year (EEIF Guidelines v8.1, Feb 2026)
programs.presc: Appendix B: air conditioners (no HP) $250/ton; air-source ducted heat pumps $500-$1,000/ton; ductless mini-split HP $500-$1,250/ton; VRF HP $750-$1,500/ton; chillers $50/ton + $5 per 0.01 kW/ton IPLV performance adder; smart thermostats $50 each; VFDs on HVAC fans/pumps $50-$100/HP; AC tune-up <65 kBtu/h $50/unit; dual-enthalpy economizer $150/ton; boiler reset controls $100. Efficiency tiers must exceed 2018 IECC/ASHRAE 90.1-2016.
programs.budget: Funded by first $5,000,000/yr of Public Utility Tax receipts (29 Del.C. 8030); first-come first-served fund reservations (prescriptive 120 days, custom 12 months); DNREC may suspend or modify at any time

Current Delaware EE portfolio runs through 2026 (22,000+ MWh verified savings in 2025, mostly residential behavioral); a 2027-2029 portfolio was filed with the Delaware PSC June 2026 and is pending approval

states.apply_c: One statewide funnel: TVA EnergyRight Business & Industry online application, regardless of which local power company (MLGW, NES, EPB, KUB, co-ops) serves the customer. Standard HVAC equipment needs no pre-approval and can be filed up to 6 months post-install; custom projects require written pre-approval before any equipment is purchased/removed/installed.
states.apply_r: TVA EnergyRight residential rebates are contractor-driven: work must be done by a Quality Contractor Network (QCN) member, the contractor submits the rebate after completion, and the homeowner receives an email redemption code to claim it.
states.rebate_c: Prescriptive unitary HVAC $80-$175/ton (up to $1,000/ton GSHP); custom $0.18/kWh first-year savings, capped at 70% of material cost, $3M/org/TVA fiscal year, $1,500 custom minimum
states.rebate_r: Up to $800 for heat pump or mini-split; up to $400 for central AC (15 SEER2+); HVAC tune-up & duct sealing rebates offered (amounts not published on main page)
states.ira: Not launched as of mid-2026. TDEC received conditional DOE approval in January 2025 (HEAR allocation ~$83.4M) but still needs full DOE approval and completion of contracting with TVA, which will implement via the QCN network. TVA EnergyRight rebates are the only active residential incentives in TN.
flags: Payment timeline (application-to-check) is not published anywhere fetched â€” speed subscore of 2 is a conservative guess; confirm with TVA B&I staff (TVABusinessIncentive@tva.gov).
Custom M&V metering duration (7-day vs 30-day) is not specified in any fetched document; TVA says metering 'may' be required depending on magnitude/complexity.

Custom rate discrepancy: current energyright.com incentives page shows $0.18/kWh first-year savings, but an older TVA custom-incentive PDF (2019) says 'up to $0.10 per annual kWh' â€” the $0.18 figure is corroborated by EPB's current business page; verify current fact sheet before quoting clients.
Whether the small streamlined-custom tier can fund the ~$400/unit HVAC OPTIMIZER without metering is unconfirmed; the $1,500 custom minimum means projects need to bundle multiple units.
70% cap applies to MATERIAL cost only, not total project cost â€” significant for labor-heavy retrofits.
A 15% bonus round expired 12/31/2025; whether a new FY2026 bonus exists was not verified.
Tennessee's small AEP/Kingsport Power (IOU) corner in northeast TN was not researched; it is outside TVA territory and has different (minimal) programs.
IRA HOMES/HEAR: status summarized from search-result snippets because the TN.gov page fetch failed (ECONNRESET); re-verify launch status directly with TDEC.
DSIRE state page could not be parsed directly (JS-driven app); program details were taken from primary utility/TVA sources instead.

No state TRM exists; deemed values live in TVA fact sheets/calculators not publicly versioned â€” 'advanced RTU controls' absence confirmed only from the public HVAC incentive page, not an exhaustive measure database.
states.notes_c: HVAC OPTIMIZER (RTU controls) is not a prescriptive B&I measure â€” it goes through the Custom incentive with submitted savings calcs; smaller/simpler customs may avoid metering, larger ones may require metering or calibrated simulation (duration unstated). CRYOGENX4 would face the same custom path with likely heavier M&V scrutiny. Very-high-efficiency RTU replacement fits the $175/ton advanced tier cleanly with no pre-approval. Payment can be check or bill credit (customer choice for incentives >=$12,000 where the LPC participates). Material-cost-only cap means labor is not counted in the 70%.
states.notes_r: QCN membership is mandatory for rebate-eligible work â€” Energy Plus would need to join or partner with QCN contractors for the residential track. HEAR will be point-of-sale/income-tiered when it launches.

states.apply_c: No statewide administrator - each utility runs its own FPSC-approved program. Dominant flow: contact/enroll via the utility's business-energy team or portal (Duke: AESC portal duke-energy.aesc-inc.com/EEB; JEA: ICF portal; TECO: PDF calc form + online app; FPL: web form then a Business Energy Expert calls), with mandatory written pre-approval before purchase for all custom projects.

states.rebate_c: Prescriptive HVAC: $19-$200/ton depending on utility and measure (Duke Advanced RTU Controls $150/ton capped at 50% of cost; unitary $50/ton Duke). Custom: Duke up to 50% of project cost / $250k; FPL only 25% of incremental cost / $250k; JEA $0.05/kWh capped at 1-year payback / $100k/yr.
states.rebate_r: $200 (FPL instant AC rebate) to ~$1,150-$1,700 (OUC heat pump top tier; Duke whole-home rebate stack)
states.pay: TECO states ~4 weeks to process a check after requirements are met, but custom programs stage payments (TECO: half at 90 days + half at 12 months; Duke custom: 50% at install + 50% post-verification; FPL BCI: after a 1-year monitoring period). Prescriptive timelines mostly unpublished.
states.ira: Not launched as of mid-2026. Sources conflict: multiple 2026 guides report Florida's ~$346M HEAR/HOMES allocation remains pending DOE approval with FDACS planning a phased HEAR-first rollout and no applications open; other sources report the DeSantis administration moved to return the IRA funds in 2024. Either way, NO Florida resident could claim HOMES/HEAR rebates as of July 2026.
flags: FPL prescriptive Business HVAC dollar amounts are NOT published on public pages - FPL discloses rates only after a Business Energy Expert engagement; per-ton figures for FPL commercial DX/chiller rebates remain null and need a direct program contact.

FPL BCI explicitly excludes 'operational, controls, or maintenance improvement' projects - HVAC OPTIMIZER and CRYOGENX4 likely INELIGIBLE for FPL custom; in the state's largest territory the only fit may be prescriptive DX replacement. Needs confirmation with an FPL rep whether a hardware controller is treated as a 'controls improvement'.

Duke Advanced Rooftop Controls $150/ton: qualifying equipment specifications (which controller functions qualify, minimum tonnage) are in a brochure/form not fetched; verify HVAC OPTIMIZER meets the spec before relying on the deemed path.
TECO restructured its portfolio: prescriptive commercial cooling ($19/ton) ended 5/31/2025; evidence for that figure comes from search-indexed content of a now-404 page, not a live fetch.

JEA per-measure prescriptive amounts (unitary $/ton, tune-up, thermostat) are behind the ICF application portal login; custom $0.05/kWh 'capped at one-year payback' is unusually restrictive wording - confirm interpretation with JEA/ICF.

IRA HOMES/HEAR: sources conflict on whether Florida returned the ~$346M allocation (2024 reports) or still has it pending DOE approval with a phased FDACS rollout; either way no applications were open as of mid-2026 - monitor FDACS.

No metering-duration specifics (e.g., 7-day vs 30-day) are published anywhere; observed regimes are calendar-based: TECO 90-day + 12-month verification, FPL 1-year monitoring, Duke unspecified post-installation confirmation.
OUC (Orlando) residential figures ($45-$1,150 heat pump) came from search snippets, not a fetched OUC page; OUC commercial rebate details not gathered - candidate for follow-up.

Florida FEECA goals and 2025-2034 DSM plans were recently reset (utilities cite 'PSC-approved increased rebates' in 2025); program measure lists are in flux at plan transitions - re-verify before building sales collateral.
states.notes_c: Duke Energy Florida is the standout territory: Advanced Rooftop Controls is a published deemed measure at $150/ton (50% cost cap) - a direct fit for HVAC OPTIMIZER - plus deemed HVAC tune-up/coil-cleaning ($25/ton), smart thermostats ($100), insulation and cool roof (thermal barrier fit). FPL, the largest utility, is the WORST fit for the optimizer/additive: its custom (BCI) program explicitly excludes 'operational, controls, or maintenance improvements' and caps at only 25% of incremental cost with a 25 kW minimum and 1-year monitoring. TECO killed its prescriptive commercial cooling rebate 5/31/2025 and now offers only custom (>50 kW peak reduction) for HVAC. CryogenX4 would have to run as custom M&V everywhere and may fail FPL's 'permanent measure' rule and Duke/TECO cost-effectiveness screens; no deemed path found anywhere in FL.
states.notes_r: FPL's PIC (Participating Independent Contractor) network is the registration gate for the instant AC rebate - an HVAC contractor must enroll to deliver point-of-sale rebates. No residential rebate found for controls-type retrofit devices or refrigerant additives; residential value is in AC/heat-pump replacement and duct/insulation measures.

d.admin: DC Sustainable Energy Utility (DCSEU), operated by VEIC under a performance contract with DOEE (District Dept. of Energy & Environment) pursuant to the Clean and Affordable Energy Act of 2008
d.model: utility(agency)-selected sole implementer — DOEE selects DCSEU/VEIC as the District's sole SEU via competitive RFP (contract awarded 2017); within the P4P program, individual commercial/institutional building projects enroll on an open basis
d.min: >50,000 sq ft building size; annual target project savings must exceed 100,000 kWh electric or 500 MMBtu gas; measures must deliver >10% annual savings based on pre/post metered data
d.recipient: customer (building owner/participant) — DCSEU is itself paid via its overall performance contract with DOEE (cumulative BTU targets), not per individual P4P project
d.assign: unknown — not explicitly addressed; commercial P4P incentive rates are individually negotiated per project ("depends on the bid presented by implementers"), suggesting an ESCO/implementer role is common but assignment mechanics are not spelled out
d.pay: custom negotiated rate per unit of verified savings (paid per MWh electric / MMBtu gas), paid after a post-project M&V evaluation period once savings are measured and verified
d.cost: not specified; likely customer or customer's ESCO/implementer, financing options exist
d.enroll: An outside contractor or manufacturer's realistic path is to act as the customer's engineering/ESCO partner developing and submitting the P4P proposal to DCSEU (which is itself the sole implementer for the whole District, selected by DOEE, not a marketplace of competing aggregators)
d.fit: optimizer, cryogenx4, rtu_replacement, thermal_barrier, solar_thermal all plausibly fit as components of a bundled retrofit achieving the >10% whole-building metered savings threshold, since P4P is measure-agnostic by design (pays on outcome, not a deemed list)

d.notes: Strongest small-jurisdiction match to archetype D found in this screen: DCSEU/VEIC is a genuine non-utility implementer operating under a performance-based contract with a government agency (DOEE, functioning in a PUC-like role), with individual commercial P4P projects measured/verified against metered pre- and post-installation data. Direct fetch of the full P4P Program Guidelines PDF was blocked (403); findings rely on search-snippet extraction of that PDF plus the FAQ document and program pages.

federal.m: Section 179D Energy Efficient Commercial Buildings Deduction
federal.statute: 26 U.S.C. 179D; amended by One Big Beautiful Bill Act (OBBBA), P.L. 119-21, sec. 70020, signed 7/4/2025, adding new subsection 179D(i)
federal.status: Active but sunsetting. Deduction is DISALLOWED for any property whose CONSTRUCTION BEGINS after June 30, 2026 (confirmed via 26 USC 179D(i) statutory text). This is a construction-start cutoff, not a placed-in-service cutoff — a project that begins construction on or before 6/30/2026 stays eligible even if completed years later.
federal.dates: OBBBA signed 7/4/2025 | Statutory cutoff: construction must begin on or before 6/30/2026 | Property must otherwise meet the existing >=25% whole-building energy-cost-savings threshold vs ASHRAE 90.1 baseline | No sunset previously existed (179D was made permanent by the 2020 Consolidated Appropriations Act before OBBBA added this termination)
federal.value: 2025 inflation-adjusted deduction: $0.58-$1.16/sq ft without prevailing wage & apprenticeship (scales $0.02/sqft per % point of savings above 25%, capped at 50% savings); $2.90-$5.81/sq ft WITH prevailing wage & registered apprenticeship (scales $0.12/sqft per % point, 5x multiplier). Eligible systems: interior lighting, HVAC, service hot water, building envelope. 2026-specific inflation-adjusted dollar figures were not independently located this session (IRS had not published a distinct 2026 Rev. Proc. figure we could confirm) — verify current-year number at irs.gov/energy.gov before quoting to a customer.
federal.sector: commercial (all EP customer types: QSR, retail, hotel, distribution, light industrial, ag)
federal.action: A retrofit that begins construction in October 2026 is INELIGIBLE for 179D — construction starts three months after the statutory cutoff. Do not offer 179D as an incentive for any EP project starting construction after 6/30/2026. For deals in the pipeline now, push customers to formally 'begin construction' (physical work test or 5% safe-harbor equivalent under 179D case law/guidance) before 6/30/2026 to lock in eligibility even if installation finishes later. Stacking with a utility rebate is generally fine since 179D is a federal tax deduction and utility rebates are a separate cash/bill-credit mechanism, but the utility rebate can affect the customer's depreciable basis or taxable income depending on rebate structure — flag for the customer's CPA rather than asserting stackability outright. For the rare EP customer that is a government or tax-exempt entity, 179D can be ALLOCATED to the designer/contractor (a third-party payment mechanism) instead of the owner — worth checking if any EP customers are municipally or nonprofit owned.

federal.m: Section 48 Energy Credit — Geothermal Heat Pump Property
federal.statute: 26 U.S.C. 48(a); OBBBA did not accelerate this technology's schedule
federal.status: Active, long runway, EXPLICITLY excluded from OBBBA's wind/solar acceleration. Applies ONLY to ground/water-source (geothermal) heat pump property — does NOT cover air-source heat-pump rooftop units (RTUs).
federal.dates: Construction must begin before 1/1/2035 to be eligible at all | Base 6% / bonus 30% (with prevailing wage & apprenticeship) of eligible basis for construction beginning through 2032 | steps down to 5.2%/26% in 2033, 4.4%/22% in 2034, $0 after 2034 construction starts
federal.value: 6% base credit, up to 30% with prevailing wage and registered apprenticeship compliance, of eligible cost basis of true geothermal (ground/water-source) heat pump equipment.
federal.action: IMPORTANT CORRECTION FOR SALES MESSAGING: EP's 'heat-pump RTU' offering is an AIR-SOURCE packaged rooftop unit, not a geothermal (ground/water-source) system. It does NOT qualify for this geothermal ITC. Do not let sales reps imply a heat-pump RTU install earns the 30% geothermal tax credit — this is a common and costly mix-up. This credit is only relevant to EP if EP ever adds true ground-source geothermal heat pumps to its measure list.

federal.m: Section 48 / 48E — Solar Thermal, Solar Process Heat, Solar Water Heating Property
federal.statute: 26 U.S.C. 48 (legacy 'solar energy property' definition) vs. 26 U.S.C. 48E (technology-neutral 'Clean Electricity Investment Credit')
federal.status: UNCLEAR — see explanation. Legacy Section 48 explicitly lists equipment that heats/cools a structure or provides hot water or solar process heat as eligible 'solar energy property,' but for most technologies (solar included) Section 48's technology-specific rules generally require construction to have BEGUN BEFORE 1/1/2025 (the geothermal-heat-pump carveout to 2035 is a named exception; solar was not similarly carved out). New projects starting construction in 2025 or later are expected to use the replacement Section 48E credit instead — but 48E is statutorily framed as the 'Clean Electricity Investment Credit,' requiring the qualified facility to PRODUCE ELECTRICITY with a greenhouse-gas emissions rate of zero or less. Non-electric solar thermal/process-heat/water-heating equipment does not produce electricity, so whether it has ANY current federal ITC pathway is genuinely unresolved from the sources reviewed this session — secondary sources conflict (some list 'Solar Water Heat/Solar Space Heat/Solar Thermal Process Heat' as 48-eligible technologies without noting the 2025 construction-start cutoff; one source stated 48E disallows credit for 'qualified solar water heating expenditures' after 7/4/2025, which may actually be describing a residential/25D-adjacent provision, not a commercial 48E rule).
federal.dates: Section 48 (legacy): construction generally must have begun before 1/1/2025 for solar technologies | Section 48E: in effect for facilities placed in service after 1/1/2025, framed around electricity generation | Could not confirm a specific commercial-solar-thermal cutoff date from primary statutory text this session
federal.value: Not published — do not quote a specific ITC percentage for solar thermal without independent tax-counsel confirmation. If a pre-2025 legacy Section 48 pathway somehow still applies: 6% base / up to 30% with prevailing wage+apprenticeship. If no 48E pathway exists for non-electric solar equipment: $0 federal ITC for new solar-thermal construction in 2025 or later.
federal.action: HIGH-PRIORITY OPEN ITEM: this is the single most consequential unresolved question in this deliverable for EP's solar_thermal measure. Before including any ITC percentage for solar thermal in a proposal, EP should get a written opinion from a tax attorney or CPA who specializes in energy credits (or call an IRS practitioner line) confirming whether commercial solar water heating / process heat property has a live 2026 federal ITC path under 48 or 48E. Until then, market solar thermal on utility rebates, depreciation, and operating-cost savings only — not on an ITC percentage.

federal.m: Section 48E Clean Electricity Investment Credit (solar PV / storage / other electricity-generating tech)
federal.statute: 26 U.S.C. 48E, as amended by OBBBA sec. 70512
federal.status: Active for non-wind/solar tech through 2032 at 100%, phasing down 2033-2035; wind & solar specifically accelerated — must begin construction by 7/4/2026 or be placed in service by 12/31/2027. Not directly relevant to EP's current measure list (EP's 'solar thermal' is non-electric; EP does not sell PV).
federal.dates: OBBBA signed 7/4/2025 | Wind/solar: construction must begin by 7/4/2026, OR placed in service by 12/31/2027 if construction begins after that date | Projects beginning construction on/before 7/4/2026 get a 4-year completion safe harbor (generally through 12/31/2030) | FEOC 'material assistance' cost-ratio test applies to facilities beginning construction after 12/31/2025, ramping from 40% non-FEOC content in 2026 up to 60% by 2030 for solar | Non-wind/solar tech (storage, fuel cells, CHP-adjacent categories under 48E) phases 100%/75%/50%/0% for construction beginning 2033/2034/2035/2036+
federal.value: Base 6% / bonus 30% with prevailing wage & apprenticeship, of qualified investment; domestic-content bonus adder 10% (rates step up through 2026-2027); FEOC-compliant sourcing required for full value from 2026 onward.
federal.action: Not currently applicable to EP's measure list since EP does not install solar PV or battery storage. Flag only if EP expands into on-site solar electric or thermal-energy-storage-as-a-service offerings — in that case the 7/4/2026 construction-start deadline (already passed as of this report if a project has not yet started) is the operative constraint for full-value solar PV credits.

federal.status: Active for non-wind/solar generators through 2032 with phase-down thereafter; wind/solar accelerated on the same 7/4/2026 construction-start / 12/31/2027 placed-in-service schedule as 48E. Not relevant to EP.
federal.dates: OBBBA signed 7/4/2025 | Wind/solar termination for facilities placed in service after 12/31/2027 if construction begins after 7/4/2026 | FEOC restrictions apply from 2026 (no 'specified foreign entity' or 'foreign-influenced entity' may claim the credit)
federal.value: Per-kWh production credit, inflation-adjusted annually (2026 factor published in Federal Register 9/4/2026); not meaningful for a company that does not generate/sell electricity.
federal.action: Not applicable — EP does not operate as an electricity generator/producer. Included only to confirm this mechanism does not touch any current EP measure.

federal.m: Section 25C Energy Efficient Home Improvement Credit
federal.status: TERMINATED. Confirmed: no credit for property placed in service after 12/31/2025.
federal.dates: OBBBA signed 7/4/2025, moved expiration from 2032 (per original IRA schedule) to 12/31/2025 | Last eligible tax year: property placed in service through 12/31/2025
federal.value: Was up to $3,200/year (residential) for qualifying insulation, windows, doors, and qualified HVAC before repeal; $0 for 2026 and later.
federal.action: Not applicable — EP sells to commercial customers only (QSR, retail, hotel, distribution, light industrial, ag). No action needed, but useful to know if any EP contact asks about residential incentives for their own home.

federal.status: TERMINATED. Confirmed: no credit for expenditures for property placed in service after 12/31/2025 (covered solar PV, solar water heating, battery storage, geothermal heat pumps at the residential level).
federal.dates: OBBBA signed 7/4/2025, moved expiration from 2034 (per original IRA schedule, on a phase-down) to 12/31/2025
federal.value: Was 30% of cost, uncapped, for residential solar/storage/geothermal/solar water heating before repeal; $0 for 2026 and later.
federal.action: Not applicable to EP's commercial book of business. Confirms the residential solar-thermal credit pathway (which some homeowners used to use for solar water heating) is also gone, reinforcing that solar thermal has lost its most straightforward historical federal incentive on both the residential and (per the Section 48/48E row above) likely the commercial side.

federal.m: Section 45L New Energy Efficient Home Credit
federal.status: TERMINATED for homes acquired after 6/30/2026. Applies to new-home builders/developers, not commercial retrofits.
federal.dates: OBBBA signed 7/4/2025 | Credit unavailable for qualified new energy-efficient homes ACQUIRED after 6/30/2026
federal.value: Was up to $2,500-$5,000/unit for developers of qualifying new energy-efficient homes/multifamily; $0 after the cutoff.
federal.action: Not applicable to EP — EP does not build new residential units. No action needed.

federal.m: MACRS Bonus Depreciation (100%) and Section 179 Expensing
federal.statute: 26 U.S.C. 168(k), permanently restored to 100% by OBBBA sec. 70301; IRS Notice 2026-11 (1/14/2026)
federal.status: ACTIVE and, per IRS, the single most broadly usable federal mechanism for EP's whole measure list. 100% bonus depreciation is PERMANENT (no longer phasing down) for qualified property acquired after 1/19/2025 and placed in service after that date.
federal.dates: OBBBA signed 7/4/2025 | 100% bonus depreciation applies to qualified property ACQUIRED after 1/19/2025 (property under binding contract before 1/19/2025 does NOT get the restored 100% rate even if placed in service later — it follows the old phase-down: 40% for 2025 placed-in-service, 20% for 2026, 0% after) | IRS Notice 2026-11 (issued 1/14/2026) is the primary transition guidance | Section 179 expensing cap was also increased by OBBBA but the exact new dollar cap/phase-out threshold was NOT independently confirmed via a primary IRS source this session — verify current Sec. 179 limits at irs.gov/pub 946 before quoting a figure to a customer.
federal.value: 100% first-year bonus depreciation for qualifying MACRS property with a class life <=20 years, including most equipment. CLASSIFICATION NUANCE THAT MATTERS MOST FOR EP: a rooftop HVAC unit that becomes a structural component of the building is generally 39-year nonresidential real property and does NOT independently get bonus depreciation; controls/sensor/VFD retrofit equipment that is add-on personal property (not a structural component) is typically 5-7 year MACRS property and DOES qualify for 100% bonus depreciation; interior HVAC/controls work done as an improvement to an existing nonresidential building's interior may separately qualify as Qualified Improvement Property (QIP), a 15-year class life that also qualifies for 100% bonus depreciation (QIP explicitly excludes building enlargements, elevators/escalators, and internal structural framework, but does not exclude HVAC on its face — however, exterior/rooftop-mounted equipment is commonly treated as a structural component rather than an 'interior' improvement in practice). This 39-year vs 15-year(QIP) vs 5-7-year(personal property) line is exactly why cost segregation studies exist, and we could not get authoritative primary-source confirmation this session of how EP's specific optimizer/CryoGenX4/RTU packages would be classified by an IRS examiner — recommend EP have a cost-segregation specialist classify a representative project.
federal.action: This is likely EP's highest-value, most durable federal talking point post-OBBBA: 100% bonus depreciation is now PERMANENT, unlike the pre-OBBBA phase-down to 0% by 2027. For controls/optimizer retrofits (add-on equipment, not structural), EP can credibly tell customers 'the full cost is depreciable in year one.' For RTU replacements (structural HVAC), the classification is murkier — do not promise 100% first-year write-off without a cost-segregation opinion; RTUs replacing existing structural HVAC may default to 39-year treatment absent a QIP or personal-property argument. Utility rebates generally reduce the depreciable basis of the equipment (the rebate is typically treated as a reduction in cost, not taxable income, under general tax principles for a capital cost rebate) — so bonus depreciation is 'stackable' with a utility rebate only in the sense that depreciation applies to the NET (post-rebate) cost; flag this basis-reduction mechanic to the customer's CPA rather than promising the two benefits are fully additive on the gross project cost.

federal.m: USDA REAP — Renewable Energy System & Energy Efficiency Improvement GRANTS
federal.statute: 7 U.S.C. 8107 (Rural Energy for America Program), 7 CFR 4280 Subpart B; Executive Order 14315 'Ending Market-Distorting Subsidies for Unreliable, Foreign Controlled Energy Sources'
federal.status: PAUSED as of this writing. USDA Rural Business-Cooperative Service halted ALL REAP grant awards (both the energy-efficiency-improvement category and the renewable-energy-system category, which would include solar thermal) effective 3/31/2026, pending a rulemaking to amend 7 CFR 4280 Subpart B for consistency with EO 14315. USDA said it will issue a NEW Notice of Funding Opportunity once the rule is final, and that prior applicants may reapply; we could not confirm via primary source whether the new NOFO had been issued as of 9/22/2026 (WebSearch budget exhausted before this could be re-checked — treat as 'still paused, verify with State Energy Coordinator' pending direct confirmation).
federal.dates: Grants originally: up to 50% of eligible project cost, max $500,000 for energy-efficiency-improvement grants and max $1,000,000 for renewable-energy-system grants (post-IRA increase from $250k/$500k) | Grant pause announced/effective 3/31/2026 | No confirmed reopening date as of 9/22/2026
federal.value: Historically up to 50% grant of eligible project cost (subject to the $500k EE / $1M RE caps above). Currently $0 available while paused — cannot be relied upon for active proposals until a new NOFO issues.
federal.sector: commercial — RESTRICTED to rural areas (population <=50,000) AND to either an agricultural producer (>=50% of gross income from agricultural operations) or a 'rural small business' meeting SBA size standards. Excludes most of EP's non-rural QSR/retail/hotel/distribution customers.
federal.action: Two-part impact: (1) Do NOT include REAP grant dollars in any active EP proposal right now — the grant program is paused with no confirmed reopening date; this could strand a deal if quoted as a funding source. (2) Even when REAP reopens, it only helps the subset of EP's rural agricultural and rural-small-business customers, not EP's broader QSR/retail/hotel/distribution book, which is mostly not in qualifying rural areas. An energy audit or ASABE/AEE-certified energy assessment is required as part of the application for the efficiency-improvement category — factor that lead time in if/when the program reopens.

federal.statute: 7 U.S.C. 8107; 7 CFR 4280 Subpart B (loan guarantee provisions)
federal.status: ACTIVE. USDA explicitly stated the guaranteed-loan side of REAP continues to accept applications even while the grant side is paused.
federal.dates: Grant pause (3/31/2026) explicitly did NOT extend to guaranteed loans, per USDA's own announcement
federal.value: Loan guarantee percentage and maximum loan amount were not independently confirmed via a primary rd.usda.gov source this session (the official program pages returned HTTP 403 to direct fetch); historically REAP guarantees a large majority of loan principal up to a multi-million-dollar cap — verify exact current percentage/cap directly with a USDA Rural Development state office before quoting to a customer.
federal.sector: commercial — same rural + agricultural-producer/rural-small-business restriction as the grant program
federal.action: Still a live financing lever for EP's rural agricultural and rural-small-business customers even while REAP grants are paused — position it as 'low-cost guaranteed financing' rather than 'grant funding' until the grant NOFO reopens. Same rural/eligible-entity restriction as the grant program limits applicability to EP's broader non-rural customer base.

federal.m: SBA 504 Green Loan Program (Energy Public Policy Project)
federal.statute: 13 CFR 120.882 (SBA 504/CDC loan program, Green/Energy Public Policy goal)
federal.status: ACTIVE, no rural restriction — broader applicability than REAP for EP's commercial book.
federal.dates: No OBBBA-related change identified for this SBA loan program in this session's research
federal.value: Qualifies for expanded/second/third 504 loan(s) if the project reduces energy consumption or energy use intensity (EUI) by at least 10% compared to historical use through building upgrades (equipment or systems). Raises the SBA maximum contribution to a $5.5M cap per loan (vs. $5M standard) and allows an aggregate outstanding SBA 504 balance up to $16.5M across up to three green-energy loans (vs. $5.5M standard aggregate cap).
federal.sector: commercial (nationwide, no rural restriction — fits EP's QSR/retail/hotel/distribution/light-industrial customers better than REAP)
federal.action: Good fit for EP's non-rural commercial customers that REAP can't reach. A bundled optimizer + RTU replacement + thermal-barrier-coating project that documents a >=10% EUI reduction (an energy audit/M&V report showing this should be a deliverable EP already produces) can unlock a larger, cheaper SBA 504 loan for the customer — worth building '10% EUI reduction' into EP's standard savings-modeling output as a named qualifying threshold for sales conversations.

federal.m: Greenhouse Gas Reduction Fund (GGRF) — National Clean Investment Fund (NCIF), Clean Communities Investment Accelerator (CCIA), Solar for All
federal.statute: Clean Air Act sec. 134 (as added by IRA sec. 60103); repealed by OBBBA sec. 60103 repeal language (P.L. 119-21)
federal.status: TERMINATED. Per EPA's own program page: OBBBA (signed 7/4/2025) repealed CAA sec. 134 and rescinded GGRF funding. EPA had already terminated NCIF/CCIA grant agreements on 3/11/2025 citing 'program integrity' concerns; Solar for All was discontinued 8/7/2025 after OBBBA removed EPA's authority to administer it and rescinded remaining funds. A D.C. Circuit panel ruled 9/2/2025 that terminated NCIF/CCIA funds should stay frozen pending litigation. Multiple lawsuits over Solar for All remain active (Maryland Clean Energy Center v. United States, filed 10/15/2025, Court of Federal Claims; Arizona v. EPA, filed 10/16/2025) but the program is not currently operating or disbursing.
federal.dates: NCIF/CCIA grant agreements terminated 3/11/2025 | OBBBA repeal/rescission 7/4/2025 | Solar for All discontinued 8/7/2025 | D.C. Circuit ruling upholding termination 9/2/2025 | State/coalition lawsuits filed Oct. 2025, unresolved as of this report
federal.value: Was $27B total across NCIF/CCIA/Solar for All (green bank financing + $7B residential solar for low-income households); $0 currently available/operating.
federal.sector: commercial and residential (mixed; funded green banks/community lenders and residential solar, not commercial HVAC retrofits directly)
federal.action: Dead end for EP — do not reference GGRF, NCIF, CCIA, or Solar for All as a funding source in any current proposal. This was never a great direct fit for EP's commercial HVAC measures anyway (it primarily capitalized green banks/CDFIs and low-income residential solar), but it's worth confirming with customers who ask about it that the program is gone, not just paused.

federal.m: DOE Energy Efficiency and Conservation Block Grant Program (EECBG)
federal.statute: 42 U.S.C. 17151 et seq. (Energy Independence and Security Act of 2007), IIJA-funded ($550M), administered by DOE Office of State and Community Energy Programs (SCEP)
federal.status: ACTIVE. DOE's SCEP page shows EECBG as an ongoing, funded program as of Sept. 2026 with no termination language found. South Carolina's own EECBG office confirms an active Round 3 (rolling applications through 12/1/2025, projects completing through May 2026), and now allows state agencies to apply.
federal.dates: IIJA-funded $550M program, ongoing multi-year disbursement to ~2,700 state/local/Tribal governments | SC Round 3 rolling deadline 12/1/2025 | SC 2024-round projects expected complete by 5/2026
federal.value: Formula and competitive grants to state, local, and Tribal governments (not directly to private businesses) for local energy efficiency/conservation projects.
federal.sector: state/local/Tribal government — a THIRD-PARTY pass-through: money goes to the municipality/county/Tribe, not to EP's private commercial customers (QSR, retail, hotel, distribution, light industrial, ag) directly.
federal.action: Not a direct funding source for EP's current customer types, since none are government-owned facilities. Relevant only as a business-development angle: EECBG-funded local governments sometimes hire outside contractors for facility retrofits or run sub-grant programs for local businesses — worth having EP's SC-based team check with the SC Energy Office whether any local EECBG sub-grant or contractor opportunities exist that EP could bid into as the implementer (a 'third-party gets paid' structure).

federal.statute: 42 U.S.C. 6321 et seq.; administered by DOE Office of State and Community Energy Programs (SCEP)
federal.status: ACTIVE. DOE SCEP page references a recent 'over $400 million in funding' SEP-related announcement and shows no termination/pause language as of Sept. 2026.
federal.dates: Ongoing annual formula funding to state energy offices; no specific SC-relevant deadline identified this session
federal.value: Formula grants to STATE energy offices, who design and run their own sub-programs (which vary widely by state — could be revolving loan funds, rebate programs, technical assistance, etc.).
federal.sector: state government (pass-through) — a THIRD PARTY: money and program design authority sit with the state energy office (in EP's case, the SC Energy Office), not with EP's commercial customers directly.
federal.action: Not a direct incentive EP can quote a dollar figure for — it funds whatever program South Carolina's state energy office chooses to run with its SEP allocation. Action: have EP's SC team check energy.sc.gov periodically for any SEP-funded commercial rebate, revolving-loan, or technical-assistance program that EP's optimizer/RTU/coating measures could plug into, since SEP dollars flow through the state, not directly to building owners.

federal.m: IRA Home Energy Rebates — Home Efficiency Rebates (HOMES) and Home Electrification & Appliance Rebates (HEAR/HEEHRA)
federal.statute: IRA sec. 50121 (HOMES) and sec. 50122 (HEAR); state-administered with DOE funding
federal.status: ACTIVE in roughly 20+ states as of early-mid 2026, but RESIDENTIAL ONLY and with state-by-state variation — some states' allocations are already exhausted (e.g., California's single-family HEEHRA rebates were reported fully reserved as of 2/24/2026). Florida and South Dakota declined their allocations entirely. No national rescission found; this is a state-by-state patchwork, not a uniform federal program status.
federal.dates: $8.8B total IRA allocation split ~$4.3B HOMES / ~$4.5B HEAR across states | State launch dates vary widely (example: Colorado's HEAR single-family program ran 11/13/2025-8/2/2026) | Programs generally capped at up to $8,000 (HOMES) or $14,000 (HEAR) per household, income-restricted for HEAR (<=150% AMI for full benefit tier)
federal.value: Up to $8,000/household (HOMES, performance-based whole-home retrofit) or up to $14,000/household (HEAR, point-of-sale appliance/electrification rebates); varies by state administrator and remaining allocation.
federal.action: Not applicable to EP's commercial customer base — flagged here per the July dataset's residential column, per the task brief. If EP ever considers a light-commercial/multifamily crossover offering, note that availability is highly state- and allocation-dependent and must be checked live at the specific state administrator's site, not assumed active.

federal.m: FERC Order No. 2222 — Wholesale Market Participation of Distributed Energy Resource Aggregations
federal.statute: FERC Order No. 2222 (issued 9/17/2020); RTO/ISO compliance filings ongoing
federal.status: Context row, not a direct EP revenue mechanism today. Implementation remains slow nationally (PJM, NYISO, SPP progressing compliance filings as of a Jan. 2026 tracker report; capacity-market DER participation timeline targets 2027-2028). CRITICAL LOCAL NOTE: South Carolina is NOT inside an RTO/ISO footprint that FERC directly regulates for retail dispatch — Duke Energy Carolinas/Progress and Dominion/Santee Cooper territory in SC is vertically-integrated utility territory, not an organized wholesale market region, so Order 2222's DER-aggregator wholesale-market access has little to no direct near-term applicability to EP's home-state customers absent SC joining an RTO or a market like SEEM maturing into something FERC-jurisdictional.
federal.dates: Order issued 9/17/2020 | RTO/ISO compliance filings ongoing through 2026 | Capacity-market DER aggregation participation targeted for the 2028/2029 delivery year (auction ~5/2026) in at least one RTO | Not independently confirmed whether SC is covered by any FERC-jurisdictional wholesale market as of 9/2026
federal.value: No direct dollar value — it is a market-access rule enabling aggregators (a third party, not the building owner) to bundle customer curtailment/flexibility and sell it into wholesale energy/capacity/ancillary markets, where such markets exist and allow it.
federal.sector: wholesale electricity market (context — pays an AGGREGATOR/third party, not the building owner directly)
federal.action: Do not build a demand-response revenue projection into an SC-based EP proposal on the strength of Order 2222 — SC customers are very likely outside any FERC-jurisdictional RTO footprint today, so there's no live wholesale market for an aggregator to sell EP-enabled curtailment into locally. This becomes relevant only (a) for EP customers with facilities in RTO territory (PJM/MISO/NYISO/SPP/ISO-NE/ERCOT-adjacent states), or (b) if/when a Southeast market (e.g., SEEM) evolves into a FERC-jurisdictional structure DER aggregators can access. Revisit this row if EP expands outside SC/Duke/Dominion/Santee Cooper territory.
